selected.name: Setup-to-payoff economy ratio
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the ratio of build-up length to punchline strength is maximally tight -- very little setup text is spent per unit of payoff delivered. Score 0 if the setup is long and rambling relative to a weak, unclear, or absent payoff.
selected.rationale: R15 spends several rambling sentences on fake-ID logic for a weak, hedged payoff ('Just makes sense really') and is dense_high_card_low; by contrast R13 and R25 deliver a full payoff in a single compact sentence and are dense_low_card_high, indicating the scorecard may reward economy that the dense model does not.

selected.name: Transformed taboo material
selected.instruction: Score 10 when controversial, crude, or tragic material is transformed into an inventive comic mechanism; score 0 when it functions mainly as shock, insult, or exploitation.
selected.rationale: R38 and R41 attach provocative subjects to compact comic transformations, while R49 and R56 rely more heavily on tragedy or shock alone.
member_names: Tragedy/controversy handled with a genuine subversive twist

selected.name: Phonetic pun precision
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a sound or spelling substitution is exact, natural, and immediately recoverable; score 0 when it requires strained pronunciation, misspelling, or an unsupported association.
selected.rationale: R13 and R43 present clean sound-based mechanisms, whereas R33 and R54 depend on awkward wording or visible textual defects.

selected.name: Fresh recombination
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the text combines familiar ingredients into an unusual premise-detail-mechanism pairing; score 0 when it is explicitly duplicated, generic, or framed as recycled material.
selected.rationale: R48 and R59 combine unexpected details in distinctive ways, whereas R17, R19, and R53 show repetition or overt recycling.

selected.name: Self-Contained Readability
selected.instruction: Score how well the joke works through silent reading of the supplied text alone. 10 = setup, cue, and payoff are recoverable without pronunciation, formatting tricks, links, or outside context; 0 = an unprovided action or essential information is required.
selected.rationale: R01 and R26 function directly on the page, while R48 and R52 depend more on special reading behavior or decoding.

selected.name: Pre-owned chestnut: the pun arrives already familiar
selected.instruction: Rate how strongly the item reads as a long-circulating, widely reproduced joke whose punchline a reader is likely to complete before reaching it. 10 = a canonical, anthologised-feeling construction, the kind reprinted for decades, where the wording itself feels standardised. 5 = a familiar template with a mildly fresh filling. 0 = a construction that reads as newly assembled for this occasion, with no sense of prior circulation. Score familiarity of form and phrasing only; do not reward or punish the joke's cleverness.
selected.rationale: The card-high / dense-low half is dominated by heirloom material: R29 and R53 are the SAME 'super-calloused fragile mystic hexed by halitosis' joke appearing twice in one 60-item slice (.276/.903 and .075/.769) — a direct in-slice demonstration of circulation. R03 ('Stopemfromfloppen', .179/.690) and R09 ('put it on the record', .462/.996) are likewise stock. A scorecard measures the machinery of a pun, which is exactly what survives long circulation; the crowd-facing dense model appears to discount jokes it has effectively already been told.
member_names: Pre-owned chestnut: the pun arrives already familiar

selected.name: Context-Grounded Wordplay
selected.instruction: Score how naturally wordplay grows from the depicted situation. 10 = the scene makes both senses available and the pun changes the scene's interpretation; 0 = a bare homophone or near-homophone could be pasted onto any topic.
selected.rationale: R23 and R54 make their wordplay arise from concrete scenes, while R04 and R25 present comparatively detached wordplay.

selected.name: Rhyme, meter, or song/lyric parody structure
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the item is built on rhyme, metrical rhythm, or parodies a recognizable song lyric. Score 0 if the item has no rhythmic or lyrical structure whatsoever.
selected.rationale: R19 ('when you're dancing with your honey... it's snot') is a rhymed parody of a Spider-Man rhyme; R60 puns on 'I'm a Believer' lyrics; R55 turns on a rhythmic 'shift of wit' pairing -- all three are dense_low_card_high.
member_names: Rhyme, meter, or song/lyric parody structure

selected.name: Site-native self-reference that still executes a turn
selected.instruction: Composite. First, does the item draw on the culture of the posting forum itself - posting, reposting, karma, commenting, front page, the sub? If not, score 5 and stop. If it does, score whether the in-group material is used as the joke's mechanism rather than as its subject: 10 when the community reference sets up a genuine reversal, self-implication, or unexpected turn that would collapse if the community frame were removed; 0 when the item merely voices a familiar complaint about the community, or asserts community membership, with no turn at all. Insider vocabulary alone earns nothing.
selected.rationale: Meta material appears on both sides of the disagreement, and the turn is what separates them. Meta-with-a-turn is dense-high and card-low: R11 (dense 0.723, card 0.249), R54 (dense 0.767, card 0.078), R55 (dense 0.892, card 0.379), R21, which answers a repost complaint with Ecclesiastes (dense 0.935, card 0.099). Meta-without-a-turn is dense-low and card-high: R14, a repost complaint that is merely printed twice (card 0.932, dense 0.207), and R46 (card 0.783, dense 0.166). A criterion bank built from generic joke craft has no vocabulary for community fluency at all, which is why the whole first group falls out of it.
member_names: Forum-insider meta joke that still executes a turn
Site-native self-reference that still executes a turn

selected.name: Delayed-Reveal Timing
selected.instruction: Score control of expectation and reveal timing. 10 = the setup invites a plausible reading, sustains it, then releases a well-timed reversal; 0 = there is no expectation to overturn or the punchline is telegraphed immediately.
selected.rationale: R23 and R47 establish expectations before redirecting them, whereas R11 and R60 expose their wordplay with little staged suspense.

selected.name: Final inferential step left to the reader
selected.instruction: Score how much cognitive work the reader must perform after the last word to complete the joke. Score 10 when the text stops one step short and the reader must supply the connection themselves - resolve an unstated homophone, perform a small computation, or notice an absence. Score 5 when the punchline states the joke but does not explain it. Score 0 when the text delivers the payoff and then explains, restates, or spells out the connection, leaving nothing to be discovered. Difficulty is not the criterion; the criterion is whether the last step is transferred to the reader.
selected.rationale: R47 requires the reader to recognise a square root before anything is funny (dense 0.925, card 0.335); R43 leaves the X/Y double meaning unstated (dense 0.898, card 0.289); R29 and R56 both hinge on an unspoken rehearing of a word (dense 0.694 and 0.587, card 0.057 and 0.040). These are among the most extreme card-low scores in the slice, which suggests the bank rewards explicitness - clarity, immediacy, self-containedness - on dimensions where the crowd rewards withholding.
member_names: Final inferential step left to the reader
Withheld final beat the reader supplies

selected.name: Formatting as Comic Timing
selected.instruction: Use 10 when line breaks, pauses, repetition, quotation layout, or abrupt spacing create deliberate timing or a second beat; use 0 when formatting is accidental noise or adds no comic rhythm.
selected.rationale: R21, R33, R42, R51, and R60 use spacing, repetition, quotation structure, or abrupt endings as part of how the text unfolds.

selected.name: Absurdist Logic Bypass
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the punchline completely bypasses the logical rules of the setup, relying on sheer absurdity or non-sequitur. Score 0 if the punchline strictly adheres to the internal logic of the premise.
selected.rationale: The dense model finds humor in pure absurdity even without a traditional pun, whereas the scorecard fails to reward it. (Rows R10, R56)

selected.name: Pun surface remains a natural sentence
selected.instruction: Composite, applies to wordplay items; score 5 and stop otherwise. Score 10 when the punning phrase is something a person could plausibly say in the surface reading, with correct spelling and no distortion required, so both readings are simultaneously well-formed. Score 5 when a mild stretch of stress or article is needed. Score 0 when the pun only works if the reader deliberately mispronounces, mis-syllabifies, invents a fake foreign word, or accepts a mangled phrase whose surface reading is not idiomatic in any register.
selected.rationale: R58's 'shift of wit' is a mangled spoonerism whose surface is not a sentence anyone would say, yet it holds the second-highest card score in the slice (0.990) against dense 0.493; R33's invented pseudo-German (card 0.690, dense 0.179) and R07's forced 'Re:LAX' (card 0.834, dense 0.152) are the same failure. Contrast R25's 'Olive oil' (dense 0.830, card 0.259), a perfect natural homophone. A judge asked whether wordplay is present answers yes in all four cases; the crowd is grading whether the surface survives.
member_names: Pun surface remains a natural sentence

selected.name: Escalating shaggy-dog buildup to wordplay payoff
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the item uses a multi-sentence narrative that escalates concrete details before resolving into a single compound-word or portmanteau punchline. Score 0 if there is no narrative buildup at all (pure one-liner or fragment).
selected.rationale: R05 (Gandhi diet/calluses -> 'super-calloused fragile mystic hexed by halitosis') and R11 (near-identical monk version) both use this exact structure and both land in dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard rewards this template that the dense model undervalues.
member_names: Escalating shaggy-dog buildup to wordplay payoff

selected.name: Register of taboo/shock content
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how far the item leans on shock value via sexual content, scatological content, slur-adjacent language, or dark/taboo subject matter (0 = no taboo content present, 10 = saturated with taboo/shock material). Do not judge whether the taboo content is used skillfully or is funny -- score only its presence and intensity.
selected.rationale: R07 (explicit sexual content), R25 (slur-adjacent ethnic joke), and R51 (dark, scatological-adjacent dream imagery) all lean heavily on taboo register, which can drive circulation or voting through shock-value engagement distinct from craft, though taboo material can also be genuinely well-executed dark humor.
member_names: Extent of taboo, shock and protected-group subject matter
Taboo, Shock, and Dark Subject Matter
upstream_parent_all_members: circulation and shareability dynamics on the receiving side (shock as a distribution channel independent of craft)
circulation dynamics of transgressive material (shareability/notoriety distinct from craft)
forum taboo tolerance and social-response dynamics

selected.name: Era-dating topical and current-events references
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the item is anchored to a datable moment or period by its references: named politicians or public figures in a then-current situation, elections, named news events, calendar moments, internet fads and platform idioms of a particular period (e.g. clickbait formulas, 'one weird trick'), product or brand moments. 0 = the references are timeless or absent; 10 = the item cannot be read without knowing a specific period's news or fads. Count how strongly the text is pinned to a period, NOT whether the reference is apt, fresh, stale, or amusing. The judge must not judge quality and must not guess the actual date.
selected.rationale: Mode 3. Composition of the corpus shifts across eras and so do the crowd's conventions, so period-pinning is a route by which submission timing - not joke quality - could drive a text-only model. R11 (Monica Lewinsky voting for Bernie), R57 (Hillary and Trump walk into a bar), R25 and R04 (Trump-era political items), R36 ('before the end of the decade'), and R40 ('one weird trick' clickbait) are all sharply era-pinned, while R08, R15, R30, R51 are period-free. Mixed because a live topical hook can also genuinely amuse a contemporaneous crowd.
selected.upstream_parent: the era of the forum's stream into which the item was submitted (its position in the venue's history and taste cycle)
upstream_parent_all_members: position in the entry stream (which era of the forum the item was submitted in)

selected.name: Traces of external sourcing rather than local origination
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of evidence in the text that the material came from somewhere outside this post: pasted URLs or domain names, block quotations with a citation, scripture or book references, SEO/marketing/keyword-stuffed phrasing, attribution of the joke to another speaker or to a named comedian, translation framing ('the original German word for', 'in X language they say'), or wording that reads as transcribed speech or lifted copy rather than written for this post. 0 = the text reads as composed for this posting with no external source markers; 10 = the item is substantially a quotation, link, or lifted copy. Count source markers only. The judge must NOT judge whether the sourcing is legitimate, lazy, or whether the borrowed material is funny.
selected.rationale: Mode 2/Mode 4: origination is unobservable but leaves hard textual fingerprints. R10 is a bare URL ('http://motherfuckingwebsite.com/'), R38 is keyword-stuffed SEO spam ('AKLAGARE.SE SEO CHEAK'), R55 is a block quotation with a chapter-and-verse citation ('Ecclesiastes 1:9-11'), R28 uses translation framing ('the original German word for Bra'), and R16 frames a transcribed accent conversation. R30 and R39 show no source markers. Sourcing is a provenance channel, entirely separable from whether the crowd found the item funny.
member_names: Imported material: links, block quotations, citations, off-genre strings
Markers of transcription or lifting from an external source
Traces of external sourcing rather than local origination

selected.name: Orthographic noise: typos, missing apostrophes, non-native phrasing
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of orthographic and mechanical irregularity in the text: misspelled words, dropped or wrong apostrophes ('arent', 'dont', 'wont'), lowercase 'i', subject-verb disagreement or dropped articles, missing terminal punctuation at a setup/punch boundary, spacing anomalies, inconsistent quotation marks, and phrasings that read as translated or non-native. 0 = clean, conventionally spelled and punctuated throughout; 5 = two or three small slips; 10 = pervasive misspelling, agreement errors and missing punctuation. Count mechanical irregularities only. You must NOT judge whether the errors hurt the joke, and you must NOT treat clean text as better text.
selected.rationale: Surface error rate is a fingerprint of how and by whom the text was typed rather than of the joke inside it: R20 misspells 'areials' and 'recpetion', R04 has 'i dont' and a dropped verb, R03 lacks its question mark and spells 'gipsy', R29 has 'the spend' and a stray 'about', R49 reads as translated, and R21 misspells 'callouses', while R30, R36 and R41 are clean. Not mixed: the same joke told with and without typos is the same joke, so the parent is a nuisance rather than a cause of humour.
member_names: Orthographic noise: typos, missing apostrophes, non-native phrasing
selected.upstream_parent: composition conditions and sourcing (mobile/hasty typing, transcription, translation, non-native authorship)
upstream_parent_all_members: composition conditions and author fluency (mobile/haste typing, non-native English, no proofreading pass)
composition conditions and sourcing (mobile/hasty typing, transcription, translation, non-native authorship)

selected.name: Defensive posting furniture
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of apology, hedging, preemptive defense, disclaimer, trend-setting language, or self-deprecation surrounding the joke. Do not judge sincerity or effectiveness.
selected.rationale: Such furniture can proxy anxiety, anticipated criticism, or posting strategy rather than the joke's content. It is visible context-management, not a quality judgment. Compare R23, R25, R46, and R53.
upstream_parent_all_members: author's practice in the format and their expectation of how the crowd polices posts (norm-anxiety of a newer or occasional poster)
poster's practice in the format (unpractised posters add throat-clearing; practised ones strip it)

selected.name: Retelling-chain positioning: repost or remix framing
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text positions itself somewhere in the life-cycle of a joke the audience has already met: explicit repost/repetition talk, claims of novelty or of starting something new, 'you know the one' presupposition, jokes whose subject is the recycling of jokes, near-verbatim self-repetition inside the item, or a punchline that only lands if the reader already knows a prior version or a stock joke form. 0 = the item presents itself as a self-contained joke with no relation to prior circulation; 10 = its relation to prior circulation is the entire content. Count the presence and prominence of such positioning only. The judge must NOT judge originality, must NOT decide whether the item actually is a repost, and must NOT judge quality.
selected.rationale: Mode 3. Where an item sits in a retelling chain is an unobservable upstream fact, but it leaves loud textual traces and those traces travel with the text. R44 literally repeats its own sentence about reposts, R03 makes reposts the punchline of an Adam-and-Eve joke, R21 opens by conceding it is a repost, R55 frames the forum as older than Ecclesiastes, and R05 claims to be minting a new genre. R27 and R46 are two variants of one circulating pun (super-calloused fragile mystic hexed with halitosis), which is itself chain position visible in text. None of this speaks to how funny the joke is.
member_names: Retelling-chain markers: chestnut status, repost framing, known-form dependence
Retelling-chain positioning: repost or remix framing

selected.name: Meta-Platform and Community References
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the text explicitly mentions online platforms, subreddits, karma, upvotes, reposting, or the act of posting itself. Do not judge if this makes the joke good or bad; score only the presence of community-specific meta-references.
selected.rationale: Jokes that reference the platform or community mechanics often trigger reflexive engagement from the forum's users regardless of the underlying humor. R04 (commenting on this sub) and R23 (mentioning upvotes) lean heavily on this inside-baseball channel, while R07 explicitly references r/Jokes.
member_names: Explicit self-reference to the posting venue
upstream_parent_all_members: poster's tenure and immersion in the venue (habitual insider vs one-off poster)
poster's tenure and in-group membership in this specific forum (a regular writing for insiders vs an outsider posting a generic joke)

selected.name: Delivery-format commitment
selected.instruction: How much does the item visibly commit to a recognizable delivery format—one-liner, question-answer, dialogue, riddle, narrative build, list, or technical wordplay? Score only the format footprint from 0-10; do not judge how well the format works.
selected.rationale: A poster's habitual format leaves a scorable structural trace that can predict reception through familiarity or platform fit, while format choice may also contribute to genuine amusement. Examples include R02, R13, R24, R33, R35, and R42.

selected.name: Throat-clearing and setup-to-punch word ratio
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of preamble relative to punch: scene-setting sentences, background exposition, first-person framing narrative ('I was going to...', 'So there was a...', 'I recently attended...'), and elaboration before the payoff arrives. Estimate the share of the item's words that precede the final turn: 0 = essentially no preamble (the item is one line and the turn is immediate); 10 = a long multi-sentence or multi-paragraph build with a short terminal tag. Score length and proportion only. The judge must NOT judge whether the build is entertaining, well paced, or whether the payoff was worth it.
selected.rationale: Mode 2: composition effort and trimming are unobservable, but their fingerprint is the preamble-to-punch ratio, a pure length proxy that a judge can measure and that is known to correlate with model scores independently of comedic merit. R27 and R46 are long multi-clause builds to one pun, R32 stages a whole dialogue, R52 runs a paragraph before 'Just makes sense really'; against these R15, R29, R48 and R06 are single lines with no build. The slice's two models disagree across both ends of this ratio.
member_names: Length of throat-clearing preamble before the pivot
selected.upstream_parent: author's practice and effort budget at composition time (how much drafting and trimming the submission received)
upstream_parent_all_members: author's practice and effort budget at composition time (how much drafting and trimming the submission received)

selected.name: Spam or non-joke textual artifact
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the text resembles spam, SEO text, external links, or repeated boilerplate phrases rather than a cohesive joke. 0 = clearly a joke, 10 = entirely spam or broken links. Do not judge if this makes the text good or bad.
selected.rationale: The presence of random URLs, SEO text, or completely incoherent boilerplate (R07, R11, R37) acts as a fingerprint for automated or non-human submission processes, representing a vector of entry completely unlinked to comedic quality.
